I am a 63-year-old woman who has farmed the same land in Quzhou County my whole life. My parents taught me everything I know, and I have watched the seasons turn on this plain for over six decades. We have good loamy soil here on the North China Plain, but the growing season is tight—you have to squeeze two crops out of the same piece of land if you want to feed your family and have grain left over to sell.

This year, I will stick to what I know works: winter wheat followed by summer maize on all 6 mu of my land. I am not young anymore, so I am not going to gamble on strange new crops. The wheat gets planted right after the National Day holiday in early October, sleeps through the winter under the snow, and comes up green in March. I will harvest it in early June, burn the stubble—or rather, till it under now that the cadres enforce the no-burn rule—and immediately plant maize so it can catch the summer rains and the long days.

For seed, I will buy improved varieties from the township supply shop. The wheat seed is “Jimai” or something similar—short-stalk, high-yield, resists lodging. The maize is hybrid, the kind with the pink coating on the seed. I have learned that cheap seed is expensive seed.

Fertilizer: I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing for both crops, then top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring and again at the maize jointing stage. The soil here is tired, so I give the wheat about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium. The maize is hungrier for nitrogen because it grows fast in the heat—about 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, 4 kg potassium.

Water: I have an electric pump and a hose. I will irrigate the wheat three times—once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The maize I will water twice, at jointing and at the big-flare stage, unless the summer rains are generous. If the rains come heavy, maybe only once.

Pests come every year. I will spray wheat three times: once for aphids in spring, once for rust if I see orange spots, and once mixed with fungicide at heading. For maize, twice: once when the armyworms show up in July, and once for ear rot prevention.

I till with the rotary tiller. No-tillage sounds nice on the television, but my neighbors who tried it had too many weeds. I rotary-till before wheat sowing and again right after wheat harvest to prepare the maize bed.

I expect the wheat to yield about 500 kg per mu and the maize about 600 kg per mu in a normal year. If the spring drought stays away, maybe a little more.
